body:
Representing geographical temperature patterns

Temperature varies across the Earth's surface according to latitude, altitude, continentality, winds, ocean currents and local conditions. Maps of temperature distribution commonly use lines called isotherms.

An isotherm is a line on a map connecting places having equal temperature for a specified time or period.

Isotherms may represent instantaneous temperatures or mean temperatures for a day, month or year. In many global climatological maps, temperatures are adjusted to mean sea level to reduce the direct influence of differing surface elevations.

Closely spaced isotherms indicate a relatively large horizontal temperature gradient. Widely spaced isotherms indicate a smaller gradient.

Geographical lineConnects places of equal
IsothermTemperature
IsobarAtmospheric pressure
IsohyetPrecipitation amount

General orientation of isotherms

Since latitude is a major control of annual temperature, isotherms generally extend in an east–west direction, approximately parallel to latitudes.

They do not follow parallels perfectly. Continental heating, ocean currents, mountains and atmospheric circulation cause deviations from a simple latitudinal pattern.

January temperature distribution

January is a winter month in the Northern Hemisphere and a summer month in the Southern Hemisphere.

During the Northern Hemisphere winter, large continental interiors cool more rapidly and strongly than adjacent oceans. Consequently, isotherms generally bend towards the equator over cold continents and towards the poles over comparatively warm oceans.

The warm Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift contribute to a pronounced poleward displacement of isotherms over the North Atlantic and parts of western Europe.

Very low winter temperatures occur in the continental interior of northern Asia because of high latitude, long winter nights and strong continental cooling.

July temperature distribution

July is a summer month in the Northern Hemisphere and a winter month in the Southern Hemisphere.

During the Northern Hemisphere summer, continents generally heat more strongly than adjacent oceans. Consequently, isotherms commonly bend poleward over warm continents and equatorward over comparatively cool oceanic regions.

These deviations are general patterns rather than universal rules. Ocean currents, regional winds, elevation and other conditions can modify them.

Northern and Southern Hemisphere contrast

The Northern Hemisphere contains a larger proportion of the world's land area. Its isotherms therefore show strong deviations associated with the differing heating and cooling rates of continents and oceans.

The Southern Hemisphere is more extensively covered by oceans, so its isotherms generally follow latitudes more regularly.

Annual range of temperature

The annual temperature range is the difference between the mean temperature of the warmest month and the mean temperature of the coldest month at a location.

A place has a mean temperature of 28°C in its warmest month and −12°C in its coldest month. Its annual temperature range is 40°C.

The annual temperature range must be distinguished from the difference between the highest and lowest individual temperature observations during an entire year.

Annual ranges are generally large in high-latitude continental interiors, particularly Siberia, where summers can be relatively warm and winters extremely cold. They are generally small in equatorial regions and over oceans.

January and July mean temperatures are commonly used to illustrate seasonal contrasts, but they are not necessarily the coldest and warmest months at every location.

Prelims focus

  • Isotherms connect places having equal temperature.
  • Closely spaced isotherms indicate a strong horizontal temperature gradient.
  • Northern Hemisphere January: isotherms generally bend equatorward over cold land.
  • Northern Hemisphere July: isotherms generally bend poleward over warm land.
  • Continental interiors commonly have larger annual temperature ranges than maritime regions.
  • Trap: Isotherms are generally more regular in the ocean-dominated Southern Hemisphere, not the Northern Hemisphere.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2026–27, Chapter 8, Distribution of Temperature, pp. 70–73, January and July Isotherms and Annual Range figures; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, reprint 2020, Chapter 9, Horizontal Distribution of Temperature, pp. 64–65.]

title: Horizontal Distribution of Temperature and Isotherms

body:
Temperature changes with altitude

Temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude within the troposphere. This is partly because much of the energy heating the lower atmosphere originates from the Earth's surface.

Atmospheric pressure also decreases with height. When air rises and encounters lower pressure, it expands. Expansion can cool the air even without heat being transferred to its surroundings.

A temperature lapse rate expresses the change in air temperature with increasing altitude, commonly stated as the decrease in temperature per kilometre.

Environmental lapse rate

The environmental lapse rate is the actual rate at which the temperature of the surrounding atmosphere changes with altitude at a particular place and time.

It varies with local heating, moisture, cloud cover, wind, atmospheric circulation and the presence of temperature inversions.

Under standard tropospheric conditions, the normal lapse rate is approximately 6.5°C per kilometre, or 0.65°C per 100 m. This is a conventional average or reference value, not a universal daily observation.

Assume that the air temperature at a reference elevation is 30°C and that the normal lapse rate of 6.5°C per kilometre applies throughout the next 1 km. The estimated temperature 1 km above that elevation is 23.5°C.

Some elementary textbook descriptions also use the rounded approximation of a 1°C decrease for every 165 m of ascent. These conventional approximations should not be treated as mathematically identical exact values.

Adiabatic temperature change

An adiabatic process occurs without heat exchange between an air parcel and its surroundings.

When an air parcel rises, the decreasing external atmospheric pressure allows it to expand. It performs work during expansion and its temperature decreases. When it descends into a region of higher pressure, compression increases its temperature.

Dry adiabatic lapse rate

The dry adiabatic lapse rate describes the cooling of an unsaturated air parcel as it rises adiabatically. Its approximate value is 9.8°C per kilometre, commonly rounded to 10°C per kilometre.

The word dry does not necessarily mean that the air contains no water vapour. It means that the parcel remains unsaturated and does not experience condensation during the relevant ascent.

Moist adiabatic lapse rate

When rising moist air becomes saturated, further cooling can cause condensation. The condensation releases latent heat, partly offsetting the cooling caused by expansion.

Consequently, the moist or saturated adiabatic lapse rate is generally smaller than the dry adiabatic lapse rate. A value near 5–6°C per kilometre is often used as a simple example, but the actual rate varies with temperature, pressure and moisture conditions.

Comparison of lapse rates

Lapse rateApproximate valueWhat it describes
Normal lapse rate6.5°C/kmStandard reference decrease in atmospheric temperature
Environmental lapse rateVariableActual vertical temperature profile
Dry adiabatic lapse rate9.8°C/kmTemperature change of an unsaturated moving air parcel
Moist adiabatic lapse rateVariable; commonly smaller than 9.8°C/kmTemperature change of a saturated rising parcel

Temperature profile and atmospheric stability

The relationship between the temperature of a moving air parcel and the surrounding atmosphere determines its buoyancy. An air parcel that is warmer than its surroundings tends to rise, whereas one that is colder tends to sink.

If the surrounding temperature decreases rapidly with height, rising air may remain relatively warm, favouring instability and vertical movement. If the surrounding temperature decreases slowly or increases with altitude, rising air is more likely to become colder than its surroundings, favouring stability.

Where temperature remains constant with altitude, the layer is described as isothermal. Where temperature increases with altitude, a temperature inversion exists. Under the convention that lapse rate measures temperature decrease with height, an isothermal layer has a zero lapse rate and an inversion has a negative lapse rate.

Prelims focus

  • The normal tropospheric lapse rate is approximately 6.5°C/km.
  • The dry adiabatic lapse rate is approximately 9.8°C/km.
  • The moist adiabatic lapse rate varies and is generally smaller than the dry rate.
  • Rising air cools through adiabatic expansion; descending air warms through compression.
  • Condensation releases latent heat and reduces the rate of cooling during saturated ascent.
  • Trap: The environmental lapse rate describes surrounding air; adiabatic lapse rates describe moving air parcels.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2025–26, Chapter 7, p. 65, and reprint 2026–27, Chapter 8, Altitude and Inversion of Temperature, pp. 70, 73–74; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, reprint 2020, Chapter 9, p. 65; NOAA National Weather Service Glossary, Adiabatic Lapse Rate, Environmental Lapse Rate and Moist Adiabatic Lapse Rate, consulted 28 November 2026.]

title: Vertical Temperature Distribution and Atmospheric Lapse Rates

body:
Reversal of the normal temperature pattern

Within the troposphere, temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude. Under certain atmospheric conditions, however, a layer of colder air lies beneath warmer air.

Temperature inversion is a condition in which air temperature increases with altitude through a particular atmospheric layer, instead of decreasing as it normally does in the troposphere.

An inversion can begin at the Earth's surface or occur at some height above it. It does not require the entire troposphere to have an inverted temperature profile.

Cold, relatively dense air beneath warmer air forms a stable arrangement that restricts vertical mixing and convection.

Radiation inversion

Radiation inversion develops when the ground loses energy rapidly through terrestrial radiation, particularly during the night. The ground becomes colder and cools the air immediately above it through heat exchange.

The higher air layers may remain relatively warmer. Temperature then increases with height through the shallow layer near the ground.

Conditions favouring radiation inversion

  • Long winter nights, which permit extended radiative cooling.
  • Clear skies, which favour greater net longwave energy loss.
  • Calm or light winds, which limit turbulent mixing with warmer air.
  • Dry atmospheric conditions that can favour strong radiative cooling.
  • Snow-covered surfaces and sheltered low-lying areas, where strong cooling may occur.

These conditions favour inversion but are not all necessary in every case.

Radiation inversions often become strongest towards the end of the night. Solar heating after sunrise frequently weakens or removes them by warming the ground and encouraging convection.

Valley inversion or cold-air drainage

In mountainous regions, air adjacent to slopes may cool rapidly at night. The denser cold air flows downhill under gravity and accumulates in valley bottoms or enclosed basins.

As a result, the valley floor may become colder than parts of the surrounding slopes. This condition reverses the usual decrease in temperature with altitude across the affected elevation range.

The process is commonly called cold-air drainage or air drainage inversion. It frequently develops together with nighttime radiative cooling.

Advection inversion

An advection inversion can develop when warm air moves horizontally over a colder surface, such as snow-covered land or a cold ocean current.

The lower part of the moving air mass cools through contact with the colder surface, while the air above remains relatively warm.

Such an inversion may persist as long as the temperature contrast and the relevant air movement continue. Moist marine air under similar conditions may also favour fog or low clouds.

Subsidence inversion

Subsidence means the downward movement of air through the atmosphere. Descending air experiences increasing pressure, undergoes compression and warms adiabatically.

When subsidence produces a warm layer above cooler lower-level air, an elevated temperature inversion may develop. This is called a subsidence inversion.

It commonly occurs in association with high-pressure systems and can act as a stable layer limiting the upward development of clouds and vertical mixing.

Frontal inversion

A front is a boundary separating air masses with contrasting properties. At a frontal boundary, warmer and less dense air may overlie colder and denser air.

This vertical arrangement can produce an inversion through the frontal transition layer. Frontal inversions are therefore associated with the meeting and vertical arrangement of contrasting air masses.

Duration and stability

Some inversions last only a few hours, while others persist for several days or longer under favourable atmospheric conditions. Inversion conditions are especially common in cold polar environments and sheltered mountain valleys.

The normal increase of temperature through much of the stratosphere is also an inverted temperature gradient in a physical sense. However, the weather-related term temperature inversion commonly refers to local or regional stable layers in the lower atmosphere.

Prelims focus

  • Radiation inversion develops through strong surface cooling.
  • Valley inversion results from cold-air drainage and accumulation.
  • Advection inversion can develop when warm air passes over a colder surface.
  • Subsidence inversion is associated with descending, compressively warming air.
  • Frontal inversion occurs where warmer air overlies colder air along a front.
  • Trap: Temperature inversion can occur above the ground and need not extend throughout the entire troposphere.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2026–27, Chapter 8, Inversion of Temperature, pp. 73–74; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, reprint 2020, Chapter 9, Inversion of Temperature, p. 65; NOAA National Weather Service Glossary, Inversion, Frontal Inversion, Marine Inversion and Nocturnal Inversion, consulted 28 November 2026.]
